entry.title: Disjoint Set Union-Study Guide
entry.content:
Disjoint Set Union (Union-Find) study guide

Oct 17, 2026 · @Muneeb

A disjoint set union (DSU, also called union-find) is a tool for keeping track of groups. It can quickly tell you whether two things are in the same group, and quickly merge two groups into one. Each step is almost instant (technically O(α(n)), which is effectively constant). This guide explains the idea in plain words, shows traced runs of real code, and ends with a practice list with no solutions.

What a DSU is

Think of friend groups. Every group has one captain. To check whether two people are in the same group, ask each one “who is your captain?” If the answers match, they are in the same group. To merge two groups, make one captain report to the other captain.

A DSU does exactly this with one array. parent[x] is the person that x reports to. A captain reports to themselves. If you keep following the parents, you always end at the captain. We call the captain the root.

Read the picture below from left to right. Eight people start alone. Four merges make pairs. Three more merges join everyone into one group. The whole structure is just the array [0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 4, 4, 4], plus a size[] array that keeps the trees short.

[embedded content: union-find forest · 8 elements, 7 merges]

The two operations and the Java class to memorise

find(x) walks up the parents until it reaches the captain (the root), and returns it. union(a, b) finds both captains and makes one report to the other. If both already have the same captain, they are already together, so nothing happens.

class DSU {
    int[] parent, size;
    int components;                       // number of sets right now

    DSU(int n) {
        parent = new int[n];
        size = new int[n];
        components = n;
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { parent[i] = i; size[i] = 1; }
    }

    int find(int x) {                     // path compression
        if (parent[x] != x) parent[x] = find(parent[x]);
        return parent[x];
    }

    boolean union(int a, int b) {         // union by size
        int ra = find(a), rb = find(b);
        if (ra == rb) return false;       // already in the same set
        if (size[ra] < size[rb]) { int t = ra; ra = rb; rb = t; }
        parent[rb] = ra;
        size[ra] += size[rb];
        components--;
        return true;
    }

    boolean connected(int a, int b) { return find(a) == find(b); }
}

Every variant later in this guide is this same class with one extra array. union returns true if it merged two groups, and false if they were already together. That true or false answer is the trick behind cycle detection and Kruskal’s algorithm below. This class was compiled and checked against a simple search on 2,000 random graphs.

Why plain DSU is slow, and the two fixes

The plain version has a problem. If you call union(0, 1), union(1, 2), union(2, 3) and so on with no rules, you get one long chain. Then find(0) has to walk the whole chain. With 6 elements the array ends as [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 5] and find(0) takes 5 steps. With a million elements it would take a million steps. Two small fixes solve this.

Fix 1: path compression. After find reaches the captain, it tells everyone it walked past: “your parent is now the captain directly.” Next time, those people reach the captain in one step. After one find(0), the chain [1, 2, 3, 4, 4] becomes [4, 4, 4, 4, 4].

[embedded content: path compression · chain of 5 before and after one find]

Fix 2: union by size. When merging, put the smaller group under the bigger group’s captain. A person only gets one level deeper when their group ends up inside one at least as big, so their group at least doubles. That means no one can be deeper than log2 n levels (about 20 levels for a million people).

[embedded content: union by size · two ways to merge a 3-node and a 1-node tree]

Together, the two fixes make every operation almost instant. The exact cost is O(α(n)) per operation on average, where α grows so slowly that it never goes above 4 for any realistic n (cp-algorithms). Either fix alone gives O(log n), which is also fast. The same page reports that choosing which tree goes under which by coin flip performs much worse than union by size.

Types of DSU

There are two different questions here: how the structure is made fast (implementation variants), and what extra it remembers to answer a problem (problem variants).

Implementation variants

Variant find cost What it does When to use
Naive linking O(n) worst case Attach one root under the other with no rule Never; a teaching baseline
Union by size O(log n) Hang the smaller tree under the larger You want component sizes, or you need rollback
Union by rank O(log n) Hang the shorter tree (by a height bound) under the taller Same cost as size; compression leaves rank as a stale bound
Path compression only O(log n) amortised Re-point every node on the find path at the root Shortest code when speed is not critical
Path halving or splitting Same bound as compression Each visited node skips to its grandparent, in one iterative pass You want an iterative find with no recursion
Compression + size or rank O(α(n)) amortised Both rules together The default; use it unless a variant forbids it

Problem variants

Variant Extra data What it answers
Plain none Same set? How many sets? Did this edge close a cycle?
Aggregate at the root size, min, max or sum per root Largest group, per-group totals
Non-integer or implicit nodes HashMap ids, flattened grid index, a dummy node Strings, emails, grid cells, “the boundary”
Parity one bit per node Bipartite check or odd cycle, online
Weighted (potential) offset to the parent Differences or ratios inside a group, and contradictions
Offline, sorted or reversed none; the processing order is the trick Threshold queries, deletions over time
Rollback history stack, no path compression Undo the latest unions
Small-to-large member lists a list of members per set List every member; merge the smaller list into the larger for O(m + n log n) total (cp-algorithms)

A full run on eight elements

This table is the recorded state after each operation of the DSU class above. When two sets have equal size, the second root is hung under the first.

Step Operation parent after Sets
0 start [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7] 8
1 union(0, 1) [0, 0, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7] 7
2 union(2, 3) [0, 0, 2, 2, 4, 5, 6, 7] 6
3 union(4, 5) [0, 0, 2, 2, 4, 4, 6, 7] 5
4 union(6, 7) [0, 0, 2, 2, 4, 4, 6, 6] 4
5 union(1, 3) [0, 0, 0, 2, 4, 4, 6, 6] 3
6 union(5, 7) [0, 0, 0, 2, 4, 4, 4, 6] 2
7 union(3, 7) [0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 4, 4, 4] 1
8 union(0, 7), returns false [0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 4, 4, 0] 1

Step 5: roots 0 and 2 each hold two elements, so the tie hangs 2 under 0. Step 7: find(3) climbs 3, 2, 0 and find(7) climbs 7, 6, 4; path compression rewires 3 and 7 on the way, then the two size-4 trees tie and 4 goes under 0. Step 8: 0 and 7 already share root 0, so union returns false and compression points 7 straight at 0.

After step 8 every node is within two hops of the root, which is what union by size guarantees (height at most log2 8 = 3).

When to reach for a DSU, and when not to

Reach for a DSU when the problem only ever merges groups and asks about group membership.

Signal in the problem What the DSU gives you
Many “are x and y connected?” queries while edges are only added union per edge, connected per query
Number or size of groups components and size[]
“Does this edge create a cycle?” in an undirected graph union returning false
Cheapest way to connect everything Kruskal’s algorithm
Things that are equal, similar or reachable transitively each group is an equivalence class
Queries with a limit (time, weight, length) sort edges and queries, then sweep
Edges removed over time run time backwards and add edges
Two sides, opposite colours parity DSU
Ratios or differences between items weighted DSU

Avoid it when you need an actual path or a shortest distance (use BFS or Dijkstra), when edges are removed between online queries, or when edges are directed and the direction matters. A DSU only models undirected connectivity.

Pattern 1: connectivity, component counts and cycles

Treat every edge as union(u, v). Afterwards components is the number of connected components and connected(u, v) says whether a path exists. union returns false exactly when u and v were already connected, so that edge closes a cycle.

Run on n = 4 with edges 0-1, 1-2, 2-3, 3-1:

Edge Result
0-1 joins two components
1-2 joins two components
2-3 joins two components
3-1 closes a cycle: both ends already sit under root 0

Two facts follow from the mechanics. Every successful union lowers the component count by exactly one. A graph on n vertices is a tree exactly when every union succeeds and there are n-1 edges.

Pattern 2: Kruskal’s minimum spanning tree

Sort the edges by weight and take an edge only when union succeeds. The DSU makes the cycle check near-constant, so the sort dominates and the total is O(m log m). cp-algorithms notes the DSU is what brings Kruskal from O(m log n + n²) down to O(m log n).

Run on 5 vertices with edges (0-1, w4), (0-2, w3), (1-2, w1), (1-3, w2), (2-3, w4), (3-4, w2). Ties keep their input order.

[embedded content: Kruskal on a 5-vertex graph · 4 edges taken, 2 skipped]

Edge Weight Decision Sets left Total
1-2 1 take 4 1
1-3 2 take 3 3
3-4 2 take 2 5
0-2 3 take 1 8
0-1 4 skip, closes a cycle 1 8
2-3 4 skip, closes a cycle 1 8 
Arrays.sort(edges, (x, y) -> Integer.compare(x[2], y[2]));   // not x[2] - y[2], which can overflow
DSU d = new DSU(n);
int total = 0;
for (int[] e : edges)
    if (d.union(e[0], e[1])) total += e[2];

A spanning tree needs n-1 edges, so you can stop as soon as d.components == 1.

Bottleneck paths. If you add edges in increasing weight and stop the moment s and t become connected, the weight of the last edge added is the smallest possible value of the largest edge on any s-to-t path. That is the quantity behind “minimum effort” and “swim in rising water” style problems.

Pattern 3: nodes that are not 0 to n-1

Real problems rarely hand you integer ids. These are the standard ways to fit them.

  • Grid cells. Map (r, c) to r * cols + c. Union only with the right and down neighbours; the other two directions are covered when those neighbours take their turn.
  • A special “outside”. Add one dummy node (index n) and union every boundary element with it. Anything connected to the dummy touches the boundary.
  • Strings, emails, names. Give each distinct key an int id with a HashMap<String, Integer>, or run the DSU on a HashMap<String, String> parent map.
  • Connect through a shared node, not pairwise. If items share a property (a row, a column, a prime factor), union each item with a node that stands for the property instead of comparing every pair of items. That turns O(n²) pair checks into one union per item per property.
  • Aggregates at the root. Keep size, min, max or sum in an array indexed by root, and merge it inside union.
int id(int r, int c) { return r * cols + c; }

for (int r = 0; r < rows; r++)
    for (int c = 0; c < cols; c++) {
        // the condition depends on the problem; here: equal values
        if (r + 1 < rows && grid[r + 1][c] == grid[r][c]) d.union(id(r, c), id(r + 1, c));
        if (c + 1 < cols && grid[r][c + 1] == grid[r][c]) d.union(id(r, c), id(r, c + 1));
    }

An aggregate rides along with the union. Here, the smallest label in each set:

int[] min;                                   // min[root] = smallest label in that set

boolean union(int a, int b) {
    int ra = find(a), rb = find(b);
    if (ra == rb) return false;
    if (size[ra] < size[rb]) { int t = ra; ra = rb; rb = t; }
    parent[rb] = ra;
    size[ra] += size[rb];
    min[ra] = Math.min(min[ra], min[rb]);    // merge the aggregate into the new root
    return true;
}

The root chosen by union by size is arbitrary. When a problem wants a specific leader (the smallest, say), keep it in an aggregate like min[] instead of reading it off parent. cp-algorithms makes the same point.

Variant: parity DSU (bipartite check, online)

Store each node’s colour relative to its parent: parity[x] = colour(x) xor colour(parent[x]). find accumulates parity along the path, so path compression stays valid. For an edge a-b with the same root, equal colours mean an odd cycle and the graph is not bipartite. With different roots, hang one root under the other with parity[rb] = parity[a] ^ parity[b] ^ 1, so a and b land on opposite sides. cp-algorithms derives the same formula.

[embedded content: parity colouring · a 4-cycle and a triangle]

class ParityDSU {
    int[] parent, size, parity;

    ParityDSU(int n) {
        parent = new int[n]; size = new int[n]; parity = new int[n];
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { parent[i] = i; size[i] = 1; }
    }

    int find(int x) {
        if (parent[x] == x) return x;
        int p = parent[x];
        int r = find(p);
        parity[x] ^= parity[p];          // parity[p] is now relative to the root
        parent[x] = r;
        return r;
    }

    boolean addEdge(int a, int b) {      // false if the edge creates an odd cycle
        int ra = find(a), rb = find(b);
        if (ra == rb) return parity[a] != parity[b];
        if (size[ra] < size[rb]) { int t = ra; ra = rb; rb = t; }
        parent[rb] = ra;
        parity[rb] = parity[a] ^ parity[b] ^ 1;
        size[ra] += size[rb];
        return true;
    }
}

Recorded runs. A 4-cycle is bipartite:

Edge Accepted parent parity
0-1 yes [0, 0, 2, 3] [0, 1, 0, 0]
1-2 yes [0, 0, 0, 3] [0, 1, 0, 0]
2-3 yes [0, 0, 0, 0] [0, 1, 0, 1]
3-0 yes: same root, parities 1 and 0 differ [0, 0, 0, 0] [0, 1, 0, 1]

A triangle is not:

Edge Accepted parent parity
0-1 yes [0, 0, 2] [0, 1, 0]
1-2 yes [0, 0, 0] [0, 1, 0]
2-0 no: same root, both parity 0 [0, 0, 0] [0, 1, 0]

This class matched a BFS two-colouring on 3,000 random graphs. For a static graph a BFS colouring is simpler; the DSU wins when edges arrive online or when the constraints say “these two must differ”.

Variant: weighted DSU (relative values)

Store the offset to the parent: pot[x] = val[x] - val[parent[x]]. find adds up offsets along the path while compressing, so after find(x) the entry pot[x] is x’s value relative to its root. A fact “val[a] - val[b] = d” either merges two roots, setting pot[ra] = d - pot[a] + pot[b], or, when the roots already match, is checked against pot[a] - pot[b]. For ratios the same code works with multiplication in place of addition and division in place of subtraction.

class WeightedDSU {
    int[] parent; long[] pot;                // pot[x] = val[x] - val[parent[x]]

    WeightedDSU(int n) {
        parent = new int[n]; pot = new long[n];
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) parent[i] = i;
    }

    int find(int x) {
        if (parent[x] == x) return x;
        int p = parent[x];
        int r = find(p);
        pot[x] += pot[p];                    // pot[p] is now relative to the root
        parent[x] = r;
        return r;
    }

    boolean addFact(int a, int b, long d) {  // val[a] - val[b] = d; false on a contradiction
        int ra = find(a), rb = find(b);
        if (ra == rb) return pot[a] - pot[b] == d;
        parent[ra] = rb;
        pot[ra] = d - pot[a] + pot[b];
        return true;
    }

    Long diff(int a, int b) {                // val[a] - val[b], or null if unknown
        if (find(a) != find(b)) return null;
        return pot[a] - pot[b];
    }
}

This version links without a size rule so the algebra stays visible. To add union by size, hang the other root instead and negate the offset: pot[rb] = -(d - pot[a] + pot[b]).

Recorded run with a = 0, b = 1, c = 2:

Step Call parent pot Result
1 addFact(0, 1, 3): a - b = 3 [1, 1, 2] [3, 0, 0] true
2 addFact(1, 2, 2): b - c = 2 [1, 2, 2] [3, 2, 0] true
3 diff(0, 2) [2, 2, 2] [5, 2, 0] 5
4 addFact(0, 2, 4) unchanged unchanged false, contradicts 5
5 addFact(0, 2, 5) unchanged unchanged true, consistent

In step 3, find(0) climbs 0, 1, 2 and compresses, so pot[0] becomes 3 + 2 = 5.

Variant: offline processing and reverse time

A DSU only merges and never splits, and two tricks make that enough.

Sort by a limit. For queries like “is there a path using only edges lighter than L?”, sort the edges by weight and the queries by L. Sweep through the queries, and before answering each one, union every edge below its limit. Keep each query’s original index so the answers can be put back in order. The same sweep answers “earliest time when X holds”: sort edges by time and stop when the condition becomes true.

Reverse time for deletions. If edges disappear over time, run the clock backwards. Start from the graph after all deletions, then add the edges back in reverse order of deletion. The state after t deletions is the state after adding back k - t edges, where k is the total number of deletions.

Example: a 5-cycle with edges e0 = 0-1, e1 = 1-2, e2 = 2-3, e3 = 3-4, e4 = 4-0. Delete e1, then e3, then e0, and count components after each deletion.

Deletions done Components How the backwards run gets it
3 (e1, e3, e0 gone) 3 Build with e2 and e4 only
2 2 Add back e0
1 1 Add back e3
0 1 Add back e1

Read forwards, the cycle stays connected after e1 goes, splits in two after e3, and in three after e0. The recorded run printed [1, 1, 2, 3] for 0 to 3 deletions and matched a brute-force rebuild after every deletion.

Variant: rollback DSU

To undo a union you cannot have compressed any paths, so a rollback DSU uses union by size only. find costs O(log n), and every union call pushes a record on a stack. Undoing pops the record, makes the child root its own root again and subtracts its size from the parent. It supports offline dynamic connectivity (edges that exist only during a time interval). It is rare on LeetCode and common in contests.

class RollbackDSU {
    int[] parent, size;
    Deque<int[]> history = new ArrayDeque<>();

    RollbackDSU(int n) {
        parent = new int[n]; size = new int[n];
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { parent[i] = i; size[i] = 1; }
    }

    int find(int x) { while (parent[x] != x) x = parent[x]; return x; }   // no compression

    boolean union(int a, int b) {
        int ra = find(a), rb = find(b);
        if (ra == rb) { history.push(new int[]{-1, -1}); return false; }  // one record per call
        if (size[ra] < size[rb]) { int t = ra; ra = rb; rb = t; }
        parent[rb] = ra;
        size[ra] += size[rb];
        history.push(new int[]{rb, ra});
        return true;
    }

    void rollback() {                        // undo the latest union() call
        int[] h = history.pop();
        if (h[0] == -1) return;
        parent[h[0]] = h[0];
        size[h[1]] -= size[h[0]];
    }
}

Recorded run on n = 5:

Step parent size
union(0, 1) [0, 0, 2, 3, 4] [2, 1, 1, 1, 1]
union(2, 3) [0, 0, 2, 2, 4] [2, 1, 2, 1, 1]
union(1, 3): root 2 goes under root 0 [0, 0, 0, 2, 4] [4, 1, 2, 1, 1]
rollback [0, 0, 2, 2, 4] [2, 1, 2, 1, 1]
rollback [0, 0, 2, 3, 4] [2, 1, 1, 1, 1]

size is only meaningful at roots, so stale values at non-roots are harmless.

Pitfalls in Java

  • Recursion depth. A recursive find is safe with union by size (depth at most log2 n). With compression alone, a chain of 100,000 nodes can throw StackOverflowError. The iterative form below uses path halving and needs no recursion.
  • Compare roots, never parents. parent[a] == parent[b] is wrong unless both are already compressed. Use find(a) == find(b).
  • size[] is only valid at roots. Call find first, then read size[root].
  • Group by find(i), not parent[i]. After unions, a non-root’s parent can be two or more hops from its root.
  • 1-indexed inputs. Allocate n + 1 and ignore index 0, or subtract 1 on the way in.
  • Directed edges. A DSU treats every edge as undirected. Directed problems need extra reasoning, such as in-degrees.
  • A fresh DSU per test. A judge may reuse one Solution object across test cases. Create the DSU inside the method instead of keeping it in a field from an earlier call.
  • Offline queries. Keep each query’s original index when you sort, or the answers come back in the wrong order.
  • Comparators. Sort with Integer.compare(x, y); x - y can overflow.
int find(int x) {
    while (parent[x] != x) {
        parent[x] = parent[parent[x]];   // path halving
        x = parent[x];
    }
    return x;
}

Complexity cheat sheet

Structure find union Extra memory
Naive O(n) O(n) none beyond parent[]
Union by size or rank only O(log n) O(log n) size[] or rank[]
Path compression only O(log n) amortised O(log n) amortised none
Compression + size or rank O(α(n)) amortised O(α(n)) amortised size[] or rank[]
Rollback (size only) O(log n) O(log n) history stack
Parity or weighted same as the DSU underneath same one more array

Building any of these is O(n). Kruskal costs O(m log m) for the sort plus m unions at O(α(n)) each.

Practice problems by pattern (no solutions)

Attempt each problem after rereading the section named in the Pattern column; that column names an idea to revisit and nothing more. Tiers are my own order of difficulty, not LeetCode’s labels, and the pattern tags are my own classification. “P” marks a problem that, as far as I know, needs LeetCode Premium. Numbers and titles come from the walkccc Union-Find list; search LeetCode by number.

Tier 1: plain connectivity, counts and cycles

# Problem Pattern

323 (P) Number of Connected Components in an Undirected Graph component count
684 Redundant Connection cycle detection

1061 Lexicographically Smallest Equivalent String equivalence classes + aggregate at the root

Tier 2: grids, strings and other kinds of nodes

# Problem Pattern

Tier 3: spanning trees and bottleneck paths

# Problem Pattern

Tier 4: offline queries and reverse time

# Problem Pattern

Tier 5: parity, weights and harder modelling

# Problem Pattern

Beyond LeetCode. The cp-algorithms DSU article lists Codeforces 25D (Roads not only in Berland), Timus 1003 (Parity) and SPOJ CHAIN (Strange Food Chain); the last two are good parity and relation exercises.

Suggested order. Finish Tier 1 first, then Tier 2. After that, take one problem from each remaining tier before going deep on any. Return to a solved problem and redo it with a different variant from this guide; that is where the patterns stick.

Sources

  • Disjoint Set Union, cp-algorithms: definition, optimisations, complexity, parity, applications.
  • Union Find templates, lctemplates: size and rank templates, weighted DSU.
  • Union-Find problem list, walkccc: problem numbers and titles.
  • 10 Interesting Problems of DSU, LeetCode Discuss: problem patterns.

All code and traces were compiled and run on Java 21 and cross-checked against BFS on random graphs. The path halving snippet and the problem pattern tags come from general knowledge and my own classification, not from the pages above.

entry.title: Graph Interview Problems: Patterns, Steps and LeetCode Links

link.title: Graph Interview Problems: Patterns, Steps and LeetCode Links

entry.content:
Graph Interview Problems: Patterns, Steps and LeetCode Links

1. Connected components and grid traversal

Loop over every node or cell; each time you find an unvisited one, count++ and traverse its whole component. BFS and DFS both work for nearly all of these. (P) = LeetCode Premium.

Problem Approach
Number of Provinces 1. Build an adjacency list from the matrix. 2. For each unvisited city, count++. 3. Traverse and mark everything reachable. DFS: recurse on neighbors. BFS: queue, mark on enqueue. Union-Find also works.
Number of Islands Same template on a grid with 4 directions. Mark visited on entry, or flip '1' to '0'. DFS (recursive) and BFS (queue), both O(R·C).
Flood Fill Remember the original color and return early if it equals the new color. Recolor and spread to same-color neighbors. DFS or BFS.
Max Area of Island Island template, but the traversal returns the component size; keep the max. DFS is cleanest (return 1 + sum of neighbors). BFS counts dequeues.
Surrounded Regions 1. Start from every 'O' on the border. 2. Mark everything reachable as safe ('#'). 3. Flip remaining 'O' to 'X'. 4. Restore '#' to 'O'. DFS or BFS for the marking.
Number of Enclaves Same as Surrounded Regions: traverse from border land cells, then count unvisited land cells. DFS or BFS.
Pacific Atlantic Water Flow Reverse the flow: traverse uphill from each ocean’s border; the answer is the intersection of the two reachable sets. DFS or BFS.
Keys and Rooms Traverse from room 0 and check every room was visited. DFS or BFS.
Find if Path Exists in Graph Reachability from source to destination. DFS, BFS or Union-Find.

2. Shortest path in an unweighted graph or grid (BFS)

Use BFS from the source with distance kept in the queue or a dist[] array: the first time you reach a node is its shortest distance.

Problem Approach
Rotting Oranges 1. Push all rotten oranges into the queue at once (multi-source). 2. Process level by level; each level is one minute. 3. If any fresh orange remains at the end, return -1. BFS required; a single DFS gives wrong times.
01 Matrix 1. Seed the queue with all 0 cells at distance 0. 2. Expand outward. 3. A cell’s first visit gives its distance to the nearest 0. BFS (multi-source).
Shortest Path in Binary Matrix BFS with 8 directions. Return the level at which you reach the bottom-right cell.
Word Ladder 1. Put the word list in a HashSet. 2. For each word, try all W × 25 one-letter variations. 3. Enqueue those in the set and remove them so they aren’t revisited. Return the level count. BFS (bidirectional BFS is a good follow-up).
Word Ladder II BFS to compute levels and parents, then DFS backtracking to rebuild all shortest paths. Uses both.
Shortest Bridge 1. DFS to find and mark the first island. 2. Put all its cells in the queue. 3. BFS outward until you hit the second island.
Shortest Path in a Grid with Obstacles Elimination BFS where the state is (row, col, obstaclesLeft), and visited is keyed on the whole state.

3. Cycle detection

The method depends on direction: undirected graphs use parent tracking or Union-Find, directed graphs need a 3-state DFS or Kahn’s algorithm.

Undirected: parent tracking. Flag a cycle when you see a visited neighbor that isn’t your parent.

  • DFS: pass parent as an argument.
  • BFS: store (node, parent) in the queue.
  • Union-Find: if both endpoints of an edge are already connected, that edge closes a cycle.
Problem Approach
Redundant Connection Union-Find is cleanest: return the edge whose endpoints are already connected.
Graph Valid Tree (P) A tree means E = V-1 and connected. Check with DFS, BFS or Union-Find.

Directed: parent tracking does not work, because shared descendants look like cycles.

  • DFS: 3-state array (0 unvisited, 1 on the current path, 2 done). Reaching a node in state 1 means a cycle.
  • BFS: Kahn’s algorithm. If you process fewer than V nodes, there is a cycle.
Problem Approach
Course Schedule Directed cycle detection. Build edges prereq → course, then use the 3-state DFS or BFS (Kahn).

4. Topological sort (directed acyclic graphs)

Reach for topological sort when the problem mentions order, prerequisites or dependencies. Kahn’s algorithm (BFS) and post-order DFS both produce a valid order.

Problem Approach
Course Schedule II BFS (Kahn): compute in-degrees, enqueue the zeros, pop while decrementing neighbors; the pop order is the answer if its length equals V. DFS: post-order push to a stack, reverse it, and use the 3-state check to catch cycles.
Find Eventual Safe States DFS: a node is safe if it isn’t on a cycle (state 2). BFS: reverse all edges, run Kahn, and every node it processes is safe.
Alien Dictionary (P) 1. Compare adjacent words; the first differing letter pair is an edge. 2. Watch for the invalid “abc before ab” case. 3. Topo sort. BFS or DFS; a cycle means the answer is "".
Parallel Courses (P) Kahn’s by levels; the level count is the number of semesters. BFS.
All Paths From Source to Target DAG, so backtracking DFS with a path list. BFS works with paths held in the queue.

Shortest path in a DAG (a GFG problem, not LeetCode): topo sort, then relax each node’s edges in order. It runs in O(V+E) and handles negative weights.

5. Bipartite graphs (2-coloring)

A graph is bipartite exactly when it has no odd-length cycle. Both BFS and DFS can test it. Problems: Is Graph Bipartite? and Possible Bipartition.

  1. Color nodes 0 or 1, starting a fresh traversal from every uncolored node (the graph can be disconnected).
  2. Give each neighbor the opposite color.
  3. If a neighbor already has your color, the graph is not bipartite.

6. Weighted shortest path

Pick the algorithm from the graph’s properties: unit weights use BFS, a DAG uses topo sort plus relax, non-negative weights use Dijkstra, negative weights use Bellman-Ford, and all-pairs uses Floyd-Warshall.

Problem Algorithm and steps
Network Delay Time Dijkstra. 1. Build a directed adjacency list. 2. Min-heap of {node, dist}. 3. Pop, skip stale entries (d > dist[u]), relax neighbors. 4. Answer is max(dist), or -1 if any node is unreachable.
Cheapest Flights Within K Stops Bellman-Ford limited to K+1 rounds, using a copy of dist each round. Or BFS with a queue of (node, cost, stops). Plain Dijkstra fails because the stop limit matters.
Path With Minimum Effort Dijkstra on the grid where the “distance” is the max edge difference along the path. Binary search plus BFS also works.
Swim in Rising Water Same shape: Dijkstra with the max cell value along the path.
Number of Ways to Arrive at Destination Dijkstra plus a ways[] array. Equal distance adds the ways; a strictly shorter distance resets them.
Find the City With the Smallest Number of Neighbors at a Threshold Distance Floyd-Warshall: dist[i][j] = min(dist[i][j], dist[i][k] + dist[k][j]) for each k, then count nodes within the threshold. O(V³).

7. Union-Find (Disjoint Set Union)

Template: find with path compression and union by rank. If find(u) == find(v), the two nodes are already connected.

Problem Approach
Accounts Merge Union the emails belonging to the same account, then group by root. DFS over an email graph also works.
Most Stones Removed Treat rows and columns as nodes and union them for each stone. Answer is stones - number of components. DFS also works.
Number of Operations to Make Network Connected If edges < n-1, return -1. Otherwise the answer is components - 1. Union-Find, DFS or BFS to count components.
Number of Connected Components in an Undirected Graph (P) The Provinces template on an edge list.
Making A Large Island Label each island and record its size (DFS or Union-Find). Then try flipping each 0 and sum the sizes of the distinct neighboring islands, plus 1.

8. Minimum spanning tree

Use an MST when the problem asks to connect everything at minimum total cost. Example: Min Cost to Connect All Points.

  • Kruskal: sort edges by weight and add an edge if it joins two different components (Union-Find).
  • Prim: start anywhere and use a min-heap of edges leaving the tree.

9. Advanced topics

Problem Approach
Critical Connections in a Network Tarjan’s bridges (DFS). Track disc[] and low[]. Edge u-v is a bridge if low[v] > disc[u].
Clone Graph HashMap<Node, Node> mapping each original to its clone; a map lookup is the visited check. DFS (recursive) or BFS (queue). Create the clone before recursing so cycles terminate.
Minimum Height Trees Peel leaves layer by layer (Kahn-style on degrees) until 1 or 2 nodes remain. BFS.
Evaluate Division Edges a→b with weight value and b→a with 1/value; each query is a path product. DFS or BFS. Weighted Union-Find also works.
Longest Increasing Path in a Matrix DFS with memoization. Kahn’s on the “increasing” DAG is the BFS alternative.
Reconstruct Itinerary Hierholzer’s algorithm: DFS over sorted edges, post-order append, then reverse.

Common follow-ups: strongly connected components (Kosaraju: DFS for finish order, reverse the graph, DFS in reverse finish order; each DFS tree is one SCC) and Dijkstra for the K-th shortest path.

10. Which template to reach for, and a practice order

Match the problem’s wording to a template first, then work through the problems in the order below.

If the problem says… Reach for
“count groups”, “connected” DFS, BFS or Union-Find
“minimum steps”, unweighted BFS (multi-source if there are several starts)
“order”, “prerequisites”, “dependencies” Topological sort
“can finish”, “deadlock”, “cycle” Cycle detection (directed: 3-state or Kahn)
“two groups”, “conflict” Bipartite coloring
“cheapest”, “fastest” with weights Dijkstra, or Bellman-Ford if there is a stop limit or negative weights
“connect all at minimum cost” MST
“all paths”, “all solutions” Backtracking DFS
“merge”, “same group” Union-Find

Suggested order:

  1. Number of Islands, Flood Fill, Number of Provinces
  2. Rotting Oranges, 01 Matrix, Word Ladder
  3. Course Schedule I and II, Is Graph Bipartite
  4. Clone Graph, Surrounded Regions, Pacific Atlantic Water Flow
  5. Network Delay Time, Cheapest Flights Within K Stops, Path With Minimum Effort
  6. Redundant Connection, Accounts Merge, Min Cost to Connect All Points
  7. Critical Connections, Alien Dictionary, Word Ladder II
entry.summary: Graph Interview Problems: Patterns, Steps and LeetCode Links

entry.title: Information Arbitrage
entry.content: Information arbitrage is the demand arising out of the absence of new information. Teaching and tutoring are traditional jobs arising out of Information arbitrage. But they are more institutional roles thereby offering little room for adventurism. The faster and frequent versions exist today owing to the Information Technology boom. Citizen journalism is one example of using information arbitrage at a fast pace-you saw something new, you broadcast it and it reached more people. Any information-company announcements, quarterly results, research breakthroughs, or any subject matter that can be broken down by domain experts into common language. These are more original ways of reducing(or cashing out) the arbitrage. Lets call these first degree arbitrages. Because the internet is such a vast space with different platforms it happens that first degree information does not reach its target audience in one go. Herein comes the role of 2nd degree arbitragers. These are less original but creative, observant or simply lucky. Cross platform sharing(which gave me the idea of this essay) is a typical example. The less presentable geeks post their findings and observation on X, the second degrees pick it up, present it with charm and post it on Instagram. Sometimes blind copy pasting it works too if the information is such. This classification I suspect isn’t a conscious choice of the actors or at least wasn’t so in the beginning.But it is shaping out of the design of internet and now there are people who operate the social media handles doing exactly this. Acting as information brokers with <1 minute video graphics. This is a huge opportunity and already employs so many users.

entry.title: The God Question
entry.content:
There is much hype on social media about the recent debate on God between Javed Akhter and Mufti Shumail. I was least interested in the debate when it was suggested because that question seems long forgotten to me. I wrestled with the question in my college days and having seen the best of debates, from whom both sides from recent one borrow heavily, the question was settled in my mind. But I had to watch because my socials were filled with the apparently winning arguments of Mufti. So I watched the whole thing and here is what I think about not just the debate but the question itself.

The existence of God is I think as old as our history. So it seems childish and hopelessly optimistic to wave goodbye to the question. It is the tragedy1 of rationalism and scientism(a post enlightenment trend to theorise everything instead of having humility to say we don’t know anything conclusively) to think that humans can live with the unknown without invoking some kind of consensual meaningless method to organize around the unpredictability of world as reflected in Voltaire’s observation that “if God did not exist, it would be necessary to invent him.” So when we debate the existence of god it is simplistic and reductionist to debate the existence of entity God entails. The essential debate is around the limits of our knowledge and how to live with it.

When I say God is our answer to uncertainty I mean it in the same sense as some pseudo/proto religions like scientology, astrology etc are answers to questions science can’t say anything about yet. It is then outside the rational domain and purely serves a functional one. The issue though is these have not evolved enough to pass judgements on out social, economic and political organisation but religions do and therein lies our basis of the conflict. That is why the question ‘Does God Exist?’ is so inconsequential in its true meaning and any debate ultimately turns on religion and its inability to negotiate with the contemporary trends. Look at religion as a moment in history where a new way of life was tried and it greatly improved the life of people. So it got codified and duplicated across populations. But over the time the slow and non religious developments which culminated in the renaissance greatly increased our understanding of the world. As a result these new ideas stood in sharp conflict with the archaic religious ideas frozen(in some way) in time. The whole package i.e religion can and have transitioned, reformed or vanished. Hinduism vanished for a while when buddhism came around, it resurfaced only later when it had also adopted the buddhist principles somewhat. Same fate has met the abrahamic religions. Christianity was Judaism 2.0 and Islam was supposed to be Christianity 2.0. Within religions too there have been reinterpretations. In islam it is by the concept called Mujaddid supposed to bring about reinterpretation every century. But after the last century defined the nation states religion has increasingly been either separated from state or kept as a hostage. So what remains of religions is little and partial say in human affairs and the codified, frozen in time laws if attempted to be brought back are regressive and impractical in current times. So all issue boils down to the tradition of revision and scholarly reinterpretation to suit religion with evolving morality to get the social cohesion it promises.

One of the terrible conclusions drawn is that it is that it is mostly religious people who have tendency to unleash evil. I don’t believe it, I feel it is a confirmation bias. People who commit crime by deception are and should be noticed and highlighted. But even allowing for that, suppose there is no concept of God. Will the evil no longer exist? And in absence of the concept of God, whichever ideology takes up the space(lets say astrology) will it not creep in our language and worldview by default. In such a situation a strong believers in astrology and laymen equally will be susceptible to crime and we would arrive at the conclusion that astrology is corrupting in nature. In fact we need not suppose anything. Take communism, it started out with it “opium of masses” campaign and ended up murdering people. So does the concept of God make us evil- I heavily doubt it. I believe people susceptible by nature to harm and hurt will under every prevailing ideology devise tools to further their cause. It is simply an error with human judgement and our inability to predict it.

Next we turn to the question, is the concept of God unscientific? It is unscientific like a cricketer doing all his training but then doing some weird ritual before he goes to play like say he pinches his thigh. His coach knows it no way improves his ability to play but I bet if the coach is any good he will never sit him down a lecture on irrationality of the ritual. Not only is it a waste of time it is counterproductive. His belief in the ritual makes him susceptible to bad performance if he is somehow banned from the ritual. So it is with the concept of God. Don’t we know many a great scientists(including Einstein) who believed in God yet no one can claim that it hindered with their science. The father of Quantum Mechanics Erwin Schrödinger writes, and I think this nails down the argument about confusion between the two pursuits:

“It is certainly not in general the case that by acquiring a good all-round scientific education you so completely satisfy the innate longing for a religious or philosophical stabilization, in face of the vicissitudes of everyday life, as to feel quite happy without anything more. What does happen often is that science suffices to jeopardize popular religious convictions, but not to replace them by anything else. This produces the grotesque phenomenon of scientifically trained, highly competent minds with an unbelievably childlike—undeveloped or atrophied—philosophical outlook.”

To conclude I think the biggest trap of the debate is reducing it to such simplicity as to render both sides wrong or at-least disagreeable. It so happens that the dogmatism usually attached to the religious side is mirrored in perfection by the Dawkins-Hitchen’s side who seem too sure about science and don’t get the social utility of religion. There is a humility in saying we don’t know enough but that which we know by proof and stands in contradiction to the traditions of past ought to be separated from the theology of religion for it to be compatible with the present. “God exists because we exist.”

  1. This dogmatism is notably similar to the stubborn reliance on past for the opposite side of the debate. ↩
entry.summary: Reflections on the God debate, rationalism, and the limits of human knowledge

entry.title: Intelligence For Sale
entry.content:
It is to be taken for-granted that creator of a thing will always hold an exclusive privilege and that privilege comes by definition. The creators of different eras have been groomed and rewarded by the cultural trends of age.

With changing technology art forms have vanished. Calligraphy and writing was replaced by printers and computers, sculpting by industrial revolution and 3d printing and so on. We now stand at the transition to yet another major change. The era where intelligence will be for sale. Intelligence at the price of sand(literally) and self learning just like that of humans.

In this process of translating human intelligence into world of bits there is something held back, something so intrinsic and fundamental to humans that it is inseparable and also can’t be replicated. That something should also be what brings about human creativity. Something as fundamental as origin of life. And it’s that something that hasn’t vanished despite the changing trends of our creative history.

Karl Popper a famous philosopher of science posits that “all life is problem solving”. It follows then that quest to problem-solving is the only thing humans will have monopoly over AI agents.

As AI revolution takes over it is that quest manifested as curiosity which will form the basis of economic distribution which is to say that thing will be what will decide the distribution of resources.
entry.summary: How AI will change our world

entry.title: The Technological Singularity
entry.content:
I think in the drudgery of daily life and general human tendency of reverting to mean we forget just how insanely unique are the times we are living in. 

For centuries we were contained by the physical constraints of space. Human collaboration was limited as communication mainly happened through language. That was revolutionized in part with electromagnetic communication systems and optimized over decades of progress in parallel fields. Computing came along to do the big math for us. That led to the emergence of internet and human communication was all the more participative, communal and efficient.

Modern human being with a device in his pocket and is nothing but a primitive cyborg and is very loosely tied into this human collective intelligence that we conveniently call the internet and spends considerable part of his time there. Still he is limited by his physical needs of space, food and fun. Now if AI replaces him it would mean that intelligence supercluster becomes all the more efficient. Because agents need only energy and sand. The AI agents collaborate and share information with each other. Like human beings today do over the internet but only faster and better. They will also be specialized tools with an interface with the physical world(think about a AI tool operating as a surgical assistant) but will be native to the internet. This rate of transmission and synthesis of scientific knowledge will revolutionize the very fields that form ingredients of its creation. Quantum computing, superconductors, biomedical research, better intelligence models- you name it. And fast forward some amount of time you are looking at a cluster of super-intelligence far better than all humans combined that just throws innovation after innovation at us to the levels we can’t keep up let alone comprehend. That will bring about the technological singularity.

Our history seems to be pointed in the direction of the singularity. It is just that the progress has been exponentially accelerated. So we were really slow in the beginning and are really fast towards the end. Millions of years ago we were taming fire, creating languages to talk to each other, thousands of years ago we tamed the animals and plants, then we learned metallurgy, then we looked up to the sky(astronomy) and then inwards(philosophy),we came up with mathematics, we invented writing, paper and printing press(That forms the base of the LLM/AI revolution) and in between fought bloody wars to see who was better(political organization), till we made it to the industrial revolution and it all led to this. This logarithmically scaled timeline of human innovation seems like a long preparation for this technological singularity.

My general theistic tendency makes me wonder that there is some force(really patient one) who waited all this time for us to evolve and breed and create. And we being like tiny little slow neurons of his universe are in the process of creating one level of abstraction above us. A non-organic but more efficient and smarter neuron. And that is universe experiencing itself, understanding itself, a self conscious universe if you will.
entry.summary: “You are the universe experiencing itself” just got real

entry.title: The Cultural And Philosophical Necessity Of Failure

link.title: The Cultural And Philosophical Necessity Of Failure

entry.content:
Failure, flaw, fault, mistake these have been antagonized in all cultures for very obvious reasons. Survival. You can’t be rewarded for putting your life or of those around you in danger. But one has to ask, was it not for the mistakes and failures that snuck in anyway despite cultural guardrails, would humanity have progressed at all. The answer is no. The cultural evolution of humans is as self correcting as physical evolution itself. So just as our genes evolved in response to physical pressures and selection so does human culture evolve as a response to correct or tame its faults. It also means that the failures are not just beneficial but necessary for the culture to evolve.

Therefore the importance of failures and flaws although contrary to popular opinion are fundamental to progress. The failure or damage done by it, as long as it is not catastrophic, is essential to collective well being of civilization. The human religions, laws, political and economic systems all have grown from or reformed through a crisis. This is essentially the idea of anti fragility put forward by Nassim Taleb.

This translates to the level of individual too. Individual failures and setbacks are more crucial for personal growth than success. There’s a cultural pressure to view failures as undesirable, leading to human reform and self-improvement to overcome them. But the important thing is social pressure of a failure should not cripple you. If it does it is akin to death (Both in line with the physical evolution corollary as well as figuratively, intellectually). For an individual having that awareness to not take the signal for error as signal of rejection is the highest ideal to pursue. That virtue is what helps one from being overwhelmed by societal(parents, peers) expectations. It doesn’t just help you navigate failures it makes you actively pursue them as opportunities of learning. In entrepreneurial parlance this is best quipped as “fail faster” approach.

In sum, the cultural necessity of failure is not merely a philosophical abstraction. It is a structural prerequisite for both civilizational advancement and individual actualization. To reject failure is to reject evolution—biological, cultural, and personal.

It is also worth noting that not all challenges manifest as visible errors or social setbacks. Some arrive as profound internal dissonances—questions of meaning, identity, and purpose. These subjective or existential failures are perhaps the most demanding. They cannot be outsourced to cultural scripts or resolved by external validation. In such moments, only the individual can undertake the challenge. And it is here, more than anywhere else, that the ability to view failure not as rejection but as transformation becomes indispensable.
entry.summary: Why culture as well as individual life needs mistakes, errors and failures for growth and evolution

entry.title: No Bullshit Guide To Adulting
entry.content:
1. Don’t be a bitch. Don’t cry foul. Play as others play.  Shed aside your victim mentality. You don’t have it as worse as you make it and life is not a bed of roses for anyone.

  2. Be kind to yourself for the mistakes in your past whether they were done by you or to you. Make peace with the fact that the shit gets thrown your way. If some shit sticks wash it and move on. Don’t carry shit with you so you stink all the fine places you are destined to go later in life. In a sense this is a test of your will and resilience to not be defined by what happened but by what ought to happen. First be kind to yourself only then can it flow towards others.

  3. Be kind to people they are like you. In your teenage high you might have been deluded into thinking that you are special. well in some aspects it maybe true but insofar as human emotions, desires, motivations or our humanness in general are considered we are same. That doesn’t mean be a person with no boundaries but just be gentle with others and all your cleverness, well pour it into solving problems. This doesn’t just unburden you of the conflicts that arise because of arrogance but it has a hidden upside. It makes dealing with people a lot easier. You become more empathetic or to quote Gatsby you can better fit into the shoes of the other people.

  4. Don’t be a pushover. Stand for what you believe is right. In your nihilistic vision it maybe pointless in the grand scheme of world to stand for anything you believe in but it does matter to you, fundamentally and deeply. Embody your philosophy. With whatever limited agency you have take a stand on things you think will improve some aspect of your community or world. At least stand for something.

  5. In matters of money, career and profession do your work diligently and don’t try to hack your way up. Think of money as a token of social credit. The more you work on something that people value more you earn that credit and use it to create the life you aspire to live. This may not be the popular opinion where everyone tries to hack and cheat to accumulate money but this is a no bullshit path where you will have most peace of mind. Don’t settle for something less by being complacent. Just put in the hard work. Money tastes sweeter that way.

entry.title: Importance of individuality and sense of self

link.title: Importance of individuality and sense of self

entry.content:
The Elusive Self: An Exploration of Existence and Identity

The profound and often overlooked concept of self has been a central theme in the works of many philosophers. This blog delves into the nature of existence, authenticity, and the dangers of losing oneself amidst societal pressures and external achievements.

The Facade of Success

Jean-Paul Sartre’s existentialist philosophy posits that “existence precedes essence,” suggesting that individuals are not born with a predetermined nature but must create their own essence through actions and choices. Sartre warned against living in “bad faith,” a state where individuals conform to societal expectations at the expense of their true selves. This aligns with the notion that while temporal achievements, such as societal success, are valuable, they do not necessarily contribute to one’s true essence.

Similarly, Søren Kierkegaard, often considered the father of existentialism, emphasized the importance of individual authenticity. He stated, “The most common form of despair is not being who you are.” Kierkegaard’s critique of societal norms underscores the difference between outward success and inner fulfillment, urging individuals to seek their true selves beyond societal expectations.

The Invisible Loss

The loss of self is often invisible and unrecognized, unlike physical or material losses. Friedrich Nietzsche explored this theme in his critique of modern society’s values. In “Thus Spoke Zarathustra,” Nietzsche wrote, “He who has a why to live for can bear almost any how.” This highlights the importance of a sense of purpose, closely tied to one’s sense of self. Without this inner purpose, individuals may achieve external successes yet feel a profound emptiness within.

Erich Fromm, a social psychologist and humanistic philosopher, also discussed the concept of self in his work “The Fear of Freedom.” He argued that modern society often leads individuals to conform and lose their sense of self. Fromm stated, “Man’s main task in life is to give birth to himself, to become what he potentially is.” This emphasizes the importance of self-awareness and personal growth in achieving true fulfillment.

The Danger of Losing the Self

The greatest danger for a person is to lose their self, an idea echoed by Carl Jung, who emphasized individuation—the process of becoming one’s true self. Jung wrote, “The privilege of a lifetime is to become who you truly are.” Losing oneself in societal approval and external success can prevent individuals from realizing their full potential and experiencing true fulfillment.

Alan Watts, a philosopher known for interpreting Eastern philosophy for Western audiences, spoke about the dangers of losing oneself: “Trying to define yourself is like trying to bite your own teeth.” Watts highlighted the paradox of self-definition and the importance of experiencing life authentically rather than conforming to external definitions.

Reflection on Modern Society

Modern society’s values often prioritize external achievements over internal fulfillment. Martin Heidegger, in “Being and Time,” argued that modern society leads individuals to live inauthentically by focusing on the “they-self” instead of the “authentic self.” Heidegger wrote, “Everyone is the other and no one is himself,” highlighting the societal pressure to conform and the resulting loss of individuality and self-awareness.

Simone de Beauvoir, a leading existentialist and feminist philosopher, critiqued societal norms and their impact on individual freedom and identity. In “The Ethics of Ambiguity,” she wrote, “Life has value only if it has something valuable as its object.” De Beauvoir emphasized the importance of creating one’s values and purpose rather than conforming to imposed standards, highlighting the need for personal authenticity.

The Importance of Self-Inquiry

To avoid the danger of losing oneself, self-inquiry and introspection are essential. Ralph Waldo Emerson, a transcendentalist philosopher, championed self-reliance and individualism. He wrote, “To be yourself in a world that is constantly trying to make you something else is the greatest accomplishment.” Emerson’s advocacy for self-reliance underscores the importance of understanding and nurturing one’s true self.

Arthur Schopenhauer, known for his pessimistic view of human nature, highlighted the importance of self-awareness. He stated, “The greatest of follies is to sacrifice health for any other kind of happiness.” Schopenhauer’s focus on mental and emotional well-being aligns with the idea that true fulfillment comes from within.

Moreover, the process of self-inquiry involves a deep engagement with one’s inner life. It requires asking difficult questions about our true desires, values, and beliefs, and looking beyond the surface to engage with our deeper motivations and aspirations. This introspective journey is essential for developing a strong and resilient sense of self, as emphasized by philosophers across different schools of thought.

Embracing Authenticity and Personal Growth

Philosophers like Friedrich Nietzsche and Carl Rogers have further emphasized the importance of personal growth and authenticity. Nietzsche’s concept of the “Übermensch” encourages individuals to transcend conventional morality and create their own values, thereby achieving their highest potential. Rogers, a humanistic psychologist, believed in the concept of self-actualization, where individuals realize their full potential through self-discovery and personal growth.

Rogers stated, “The curious paradox is that when I accept myself just as I am, then I can change.” This highlights the importance of self-acceptance as a precursor to genuine personal development. By embracing one’s true self and committing to personal growth, individuals can lead more authentic and fulfilling lives.

Conclusion

The exploration of the self and its significance in human existence is a recurring theme in philosophy. From existentialists like Sartre and Kierkegaard to modern thinkers like Fromm, Jung, and Rogers, the importance of maintaining a strong and authentic sense of self has been emphasized. These philosophers challenge us to look beyond superficial markers of success and consider the deeper aspects of identity and fulfillment.

Their insights call for a reevaluation of our values and priorities. By recognizing the profound significance of the self, we can ensure that our pursuit of success does not come at the expense of our true identity. This understanding ultimately leads to a more authentic and meaningful life, where personal growth and self-awareness are prioritised over societal expectations and external achievements.
entry.summary: preserving self in a world constantly trying to change you

entry.title: Adjusting to reality
entry.content:
Reality is ugly, boring and mundane. It is mondays and fridays and weekdays and weekends. In the formative years of an individual society engages one in simulations of reality.  In school one is sheltered from the ugliness of the world. Then college where reality is accounted for but in a very distorted form. Then we are thrown into work where the rough edges are smoothened by a formal jargon and scheduled outbursts of joy . All this to shelter us from the  fundamental reality. The pangs of which are felt on a usual Sunday evening. The longer one is prevented from the thought the longer one strays away from it. Trapped in a maze of desires that are programmed into us. But what is the fundamental reality. It is the bitter truth of the world. The ugliness of it. This world is a prison. We came here not from will and will leave as such. Things happen to us more than we make them happen. There is limited agency an individual has. Truth is that the freedom of individual is insatiable and the system can only allow so little of it. 

We may have decorated our world view but it’s only matter of time before the house of cards falls.

The sooner you adjust to that truth sooner you can account for it. Make genuine bonds without being deluded. Make peace with the fact that this world is designed to hurt you, test you, put you down. And anytime you feel good-any odd morning when the sun shines and you feel great be grateful for that.
